echoes.note: Paul reasons 'from the Scriptures' that the Christ 'had to suffer'; the Suffering Servant is the natural scriptural ground for a suffering Messiah, a recurrent NT proof-text. Volume modest in the narrative summary itself but thematic coherence with the synagogue argument is strong.

'rise again from the dead' echoes the psalm's 'you will not abandon my soul to Sheol,' the standard apostolic resurrection proof from Scripture (cf. its explicit use in earlier Acts speeches). Recurrence high in Luke-Acts.
'rise again' may glance at 'on the third day he will raise us up'; verbal contact is thin and the third-day motif is not stated here, so the link is faint and contested.

The charge that Paul proclaims 'another king, Jesus' resonates with the psalm's rulers raging against the LORD and his Anointed; Luke elsewhere cites Psalm 2, so recurrence supports a faint background, though no quotation is made here.
'another king' set against Caesar's decrees may evoke the everlasting dominion given to the son of man, but verbal volume is negligible.
The Beroeans 'examining the Scriptures daily' figurally images the blessed one who meditates on the law day and night; thematic coherence only, no verbal borrowing.
Daily reading and searching of the written word loosely recalls the king's charge to read the law all his days; very faint.

Paul's spirit 'provoked' (paroxynein) at a city full of idols echoes the LXX of Israel provoking God to anger with their idols, the same verb-field; thematic coherence between human and divine zeal against idolatry is strong.
A 'city full of idols' matches Wisdom's diatribe on the proliferation of cult images; deuterocanonical idol-polemic is the closest contemporary parallel and frames the whole Athens episode.
The lifeless 'idols' that provoke Paul evoke the classic psalm of handmade gods of silver and gold that cannot see or hear; recurrence of this polemic across the Psalter is high.
Parallel idol-polemic to Psalm 115; included for completeness as a recurrent OT topos behind the scene.
Isaiah's extended mockery of the craftsman who fashions a god stands behind both Paul's revulsion here and his later argument that the divine is not 'engraved by art'; sets up vv.29.
Jeremiah's contrast of dead idols with the living Creator anticipates Paul's pivot from idols to the God who made all; thematic, not verbal.
'The God who made the world and all things in it' is creation-monotheism rooted in the opening of Genesis; high volume and thematic coherence, the foundation of the whole sermon.

Isaiah's God who 'created the heavens... gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk in it' tightly combines both of Paul's claims: maker of the world (v.24) and giver of life and breath (v.25). Strong verbal and conceptual overlap.
'made the heaven and the earth, the sea and all that is in them' is echoed in 'made the world and all things in it... Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent creation formula.
'who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them' parallels v.24's creation summary; recurrence of the formula raises confidence.
'You made heaven... the earth and all that is on it... and you give life to them all' parallels both creation and life-giving themes; included as a recurrent OT confession.
'Lord of heaven and earth' (v.24) echoes 'God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth'; faint title-level contact.
'heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in it' supports 'Lord of heaven and earth'; recurrent title.

Solomon's 'heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house I have built' directly grounds 'does not dwell in temples made with hands.' Strong thematic coherence at the dedication of the very institution Paul relativizes.

'Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool; what house will you build for me?' is the prophetic charter for 'does not dwell in temples made with hands' and for needing nothing from human hands; quoted by Stephen in Acts 7, so recurrence in Acts is high.
Parallel to 1 Kings 8:27, the same temple-cannot-contain-God confession behind v.24.

'If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine' grounds v.25, that God is not 'served by human hands as though he needed anything'; strong thematic coherence with sacrificial critique.
'He himself gives to all life and breath' echoes God breathing the breath of life into the man; foundational creation text for the life-giver claim.
'In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind' closely matches 'gives to all life and breath.'
'The breath of the Almighty gives me life' parallels v.25's life and breath; recurrent wisdom motif.
'God of the spirits of all flesh' supports the universal life-giver theme of v.25.
The high and lofty One who nonetheless gives breath ('the breath that I have made') touches v.25; faint.

'When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance... he fixed the boundaries of the peoples' is the key text behind v.26, God making every nation and 'fixing the boundaries of their dwellings.' Strong verbal and conceptual coherence.
'Made from one... every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth' draws on the creation and filling of the earth from the one human pair.
The Table of Nations, all peoples spreading 'from one' after the flood, underlies the unity-of-nations claim in v.26.
'Determined appointed seasons' may glance at the luminaries set 'for seasons'; faint, since the sense here is more likely the epochs of nations.
'He makes nations great, and destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away' parallels v.26's sovereign setting of appointed times and boundaries for peoples.
'You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth' directly supports 'the boundaries of their dwellings' in v.26.
'You will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' underlies v.27, that the nations 'should seek the Lord... and find him.'
'Seek the LORD while he may be found' parallels v.27's seek-and-find; recurrent prophetic summons.
'You will seek me and find me, when you seek with all your heart' parallels v.27; recurrent seek-and-find formula.
'The LORD is near to all who call on him' grounds 'he is not far from each one of us' (v.27).
'Am I a God near at hand... and not a God far off? Do I not fill heaven and earth?' closely supports 'not far from each one of us' and the immanence of vv.27-28.
'What nation has a god so near to it as the LORD?' supports the nearness theme of v.27; faint.
'To whom will you liken God?... a craftsman casts an idol, a goldsmith overlays it with gold' directly grounds v.29, that the Divine Nature is not 'like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art.'
The craftsman who fashions a god from wood/metal stands behind v.29's rejection of images 'engraved by art and design of man.'
Idols 'the work of human hands, wood and stone, which neither see nor hear' parallels v.29's gold, silver, and stone made by human craft.
'To whom will you liken me?... they hire a goldsmith who makes it into a god' parallels v.29; recurrent Isaianic idol-polemic.

Wisdom's critique that people who admired the world's beauty failed to find its Maker, yet are 'not to be excused' because they could seek and find, closely tracks vv.24-29 (knowing the Creator from creation, seeking and finding). The deuterocanonical natural-theology bridge is the nearest analogue to the whole Areopagus argument.

'Miserable... who called gods the works of human hands, gold and silver fashioned with skill, and likenesses of animals, or useless stone' is verbally very close to v.29's gold, silver, and stone shaped by human art.
'You overlook the sins of men, that they may repent' parallels v.30, God 'overlooked' the times of ignorance and now commands repentance.
Faint contact with the call to overlook ignorance and turn; weak link to v.30.
'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world in righteousness' is almost verbatim with v.31, that God 'will judge the world in righteousness.' High volume.
'He will judge the world in righteousness' is a near-exact verbal parallel to v.31; recurrence of this formula across the Psalter strengthens the link.
'He comes to judge the earth; he will judge the world with righteousness' is the third near-identical parallel to v.31, confirming a fixed liturgical formula behind Paul's words.
'He will judge the peoples with equity' reinforces the universal-righteous-judgment theme of v.31.
Judgment 'by the man whom he has ordained' evokes the installed/anointed son to whom the nations are given; coherent with the appointed agent of v.31.
Judgment of the world entrusted to 'the man' (anthropos) recalls the son of man given everlasting dominion and judgment; supports the human appointed judge of v.31.
'God will bring every deed into judgment' supports the coming-judgment theme of v.31; faint, no verbal contact.

The Athenians' reaction to 'the resurrection of the dead' brushes the OT bodily-resurrection hope of those who 'sleep in the dust' awakening; thematic background only, no verbal borrowing in the narrative response.
'Your dead shall live... the earth will give birth to the dead' is the prophetic resurrection hope behind the doctrine the philosophers mock; faint.
